title: AC Circuits
summary: Alternating current is described by rms values ($V_{rms}=V_0/\sqrt2$). Inductors and capacitors oppose AC through reactance ($X_L=\omega L$, $X_C=1/\omega C$). A series RLC circuit has impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$ and resonates at $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 14–15.)

alternating current.plain: Current that reverses direction back and forth, many times a second.
alternating current.in_class: $I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t)$; household power is AC.

RMS.plain: A kind of average that gives the effective value of an AC quantity.
RMS.in_class: $V_{rms} = V_0/\sqrt{2}$; it's what a meter reads and what sets power.

reactance.plain: The AC 'resistance' of a capacitor or inductor.

impedance.plain: The total opposition to AC current from resistance and reactance combined.
impedance.in_class: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$; the AC version of resistance.

resonance.plain: The frequency where an AC circuit responds most strongly.

phasor.plain: A rotating arrow that represents an oscillating voltage or current.
phasor.in_class: Lets you add AC quantities that are out of phase like vectors.

power factor.plain: How much of the AC power actually does useful work.
power factor.in_class: $\cos\phi$, where $\phi$ is the phase angle between voltage and current.

concept_sections.heading: Inductance
concept_sections.explanation: An inductor resists changes in current by inducing a back-EMF $\mathcal{E} = -L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$. It stores energy in its magnetic field, $U = \tfrac12 L I^2$. Inductance $L$ is measured in henries (H).

concept_sections.heading: AC and rms values
concept_sections.explanation: Household current alternates sinusoidally. Because it swings positive and negative, we quote the root-mean-square value: $V_{rms} = V_0/\sqrt{2}$ (and likewise for current). '120 V' outlets actually peak near 170 V. rms values let AC power formulas look like DC ones.

concept_sections.heading: Reactance
concept_sections.explanation: Inductors and capacitors oppose AC without dissipating energy, through reactance: $X_L = \omega L$ (inductors block high frequencies) and $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$ (capacitors block low frequencies), where $\omega = 2\pi f$. Both are measured in ohms.

concept_sections.heading: Impedance of a series RLC
concept_sections.explanation: Resistance and the two reactances combine into impedance $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, and Ohm's law becomes $V_{rms} = I_{rms} Z$. The reactances partly cancel because inductor and capacitor voltages are out of phase.

concept_sections.heading: Resonance
concept_sections.explanation: When $X_L = X_C$ the reactances cancel, $Z$ is minimum ($=R$), and current peaks. This happens at the resonant frequency $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ (or $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$) — how a radio selects one station.

real_world_examples.title: Tuning a radio
real_world_examples.scenario: You turn a dial to pick one station.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The dial changes $C$, shifting the resonant frequency $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ so the circuit responds strongly to just one broadcast frequency.

real_world_examples.title: Phone charger / adapter
real_world_examples.scenario: A charger converts wall AC to low-voltage DC.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: It uses rms voltages and a transformer, then rectifies and smooths with capacitors whose reactance $X_C$ filters the ripple.

real_world_examples.title: Fluorescent light ballast
real_world_examples.scenario: A tube light has a 'ballast' inside.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: An inductor's reactance $X_L = \omega L$ limits the current through the tube, preventing it from drawing a destructive surge.

problems.prompt: An AC source has peak voltage $V_0 = 170$ V. Find the rms voltage.
An inductor $L = 2.0$ H carries $3.0$ A. Find the energy stored.
Find the inductive reactance of $L = 0.10$ H at $\omega = 377$ rad/s.
Find the capacitive reactance of $C = 10\ \mu\text{F}$ at $\omega = 377$ rad/s.
Find the resonant frequency of a circuit with $L = 1.0$ mH and $C = 1.0\ \mu\text{F}$.
A series circuit has $R = 30\ \Omega$, $X_L = 40\ \Omega$, $X_C = 0$. Find the impedance.
An AC source $V_{rms} = 120$ V drives an impedance $Z = 60\ \Omega$. Find the rms current.
problems.hint: Ohm's law for AC uses impedance.

problems.prompt: A series RLC circuit has $R = 40\ \Omega$, $X_L = 60\ \Omega$, $X_C = 30\ \Omega$. Find the impedance.
problems.hint: Combine the reactances first, then use the impedance formula.

problems.prompt: In that circuit ($Z = 50\ \Omega$, $R = 40\ \Omega$) the rms current is $2.0$ A. Find the average power dissipated.
solution_steps: Only the resistor dissipates power: $P = I_{rms}^2 R$.
problems.hint: Average power is dissipated only in $R$: $P = I_{rms}^2 R$.

problems.prompt: A $1.0\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $100$ V is connected across a $1.0$ mH inductor (LC circuit). Find the peak current in the oscillation.
solution_steps: Energy conservation: $\tfrac12 C V^2 = \tfrac12 L I^2$, so $I = V\sqrt{C/L}$.
problems.hint: All the capacitor's energy becomes the inductor's: $\tfrac12 CV^2 = \tfrac12 LI^2$.
